title: What someone said
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: sē MEANS THE SPEAKER AND eum MEANS SOMEBODY ELSE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE MODULE. dīcit sē venīre is 'he says HE HIMSELF is coming'; dīcit eum venīre is 'he says SOMEONE ELSE is coming'. One word decides it, and English needs a whole clause of context to do the same job — so every reported sentence in Latin makes you settle something English lets you leave vague. Getting it wrong produces correct Latin with the wrong meaning, which is the worst kind of error there is.

THE CONSTRUCTION IS M3's, UNCHANGED: the reported clause's subject goes into the accusative, its verb becomes an infinitive, and NOTHING JOINS THE TWO HALVES. There is still no word for 'that', and the mistake plate is still the English quod clause — for the second module running, because it is the shape an English speaker will keep reaching for and quod is already L1-M9's 'because'.

THE INFINITIVE'S TENSE IS RELATIVE TO THE REPORTING VERB. dīxit sē venīre is 'he said he WAS coming' — present infinitive, the same time as the saying. dīxit sē vēnisse is 'he said he HAD come' — perfect infinitive, earlier than the saying. English's two tenses are one step apart in Latin and the step is inside the INFINITIVE rather than in dīxit, which is the one place an English speaker will not look. The perfect infinitive is built on the perfect stem: vēnī gives vēnisse, lēgī gives lēgisse, errāvī gives errāvisse.

negō IS 'I SAY THAT … NOT', ONE WORD FOR TWO, and there is no nōn anywhere in it. This is the third place in the course where Latin puts a negative inside a verb — L1-M3's nōlō and L2-M9's mālō are the others — and naming all three together turns three exceptions into one habit. Adding nōn to negat gives you two negatives, which cancel exactly as they do in careful English.

suus IS THE FIRST POSSESSIVE THIS COURSE HAS TAUGHT, AND IT IS REFLEXIVE. L2-M2 said out loud that no Latin word in this course carried 'my', because Latin leaves obvious possession out. suus means the SUBJECT's own — librum suum legit, 'he is reading his own book' — and it agrees with what is owned rather than with who owns it. eius ('his', meaning somebody else's) and meus are named here and written nowhere: one module cannot open a possessive system and a reflexive at the same time, and the reflexive is the one reported speech needs.

words.note: 'He says' — dīcō 'I say', dīcit 'he says', dīxit 'he said'. English 'dictate' and 'verdict' come from it.
'Himself, herself' — and it means the person who is doing the SAYING. M3's eum means somebody else, and that one word is the whole difference.
'To come' — veniō's infinitive, and the shape a reported clause needs. L1-M9's verb.

sentences.trap: sē means the speaker. This is M3's accusative and infinitive with one word changed, and that word decides who is coming — Latin settles in three letters what English needs a paragraph of context for.
sentences.sound: DĪ-cit SĒ ve-NĪ-re. Both dīcit and sē carry a long vowel, and sē is a whole word made of one.

English moves the tense of the reported verb and Latin moves it too, but inside the infinitive, which is the one place an English speaker will not look.

The present infinitive means 'at the same time', whenever that was — its tense is relative and not absolute.

sentences.trap: This course has taught NO possessive at all until now — L2-M2 said so out loud, because three of its cues said 'my' and no Latin word carried it. suus is the first, and it arrives REFLEXIVE: it means the subject's own. eius, 'his' meaning somebody else's, is a different word and this course does not write it.

words.note: 'He says' — dīcō 'I say', dīcit 'he says', dīxit 'he said'. English 'dictate' and 'verdict' come from it.
'Book', and here it is the accusative of the reported clause rather than the object of anything.
'His own, her own' — and 'own' is the whole point: it belongs to the subject of the sentence. It agrees with what is owned, not with who owns it: suum, suam, suōs.
'Heavy' — L2-M2's gravis in the object shape, agreeing with librum along with suum.
'To be' — sum's infinitive. M3 opened it, and L2-M5 named it and wrote it nowhere.

sentences.trap: Three words agreeing inside a reported clause: librum, suum and gravem all take the accusative because the clause is reported, and all three describe the same book. This is M3's construction and this module's possessive arriving in one sentence, and there is nothing new in it except the combination.

sentences.display: Negat sē errāvisse; ego tamen putō eum errāvisse.
sentences.cue: He says he did not make a mistake; I think he did, though.
sentences.literal: he-denies himself to-have-erred I however I-think him to-have-erred

words.note: 'He denies' — negō, negat, with the negative inside the verb and no nōn anywhere.
'Himself, herself' — and it means the person who is doing the SAYING. M3's eum means somebody else, and that one word is the whole difference.
'To have made a mistake' — the perfect infinitive of L2-M8's errō: errāvī, errāvisse. The regular perfect, which is not the common one.
'I' — and putō already says it. Here it carries the contrast between what he claims and what I think, which is the one job a pronoun has.
'However', and it comes SECOND in its clause. M3's word, and the sixth of six that must.
'I think': putō, putat. M3's verb.
'Him' — is, ea, id, the colourless pointing word M3 opened. In reported speech it means someone OTHER than the speaker.
'To have made a mistake' — the same perfect infinitive, and this time about HIM rather than about the speaker.

sentences.trap: The same infinitive twice with a different pronoun each time, and that is the whole module in one line: sē in his report because he is talking about himself, eum in mine because I am talking about him. Change the pronoun and you change who was wrong.
sentences.sound: NE-gat SĒ er-rā-VIS-se; E-go TA-men PU-tō E-um er-rā-VIS-se. Sixteen syllables and the two halves end on the same word.

variations.display: Negat sē errāvisse; putō tamen eum errāvisse.

mistake.display: Negat sē errāvisse; ego tamen putō sē errāvisse.
mistake.why: sē used in the second clause, where the speaker is me and the person being discussed is him. sē always points at the subject of its OWN clause, so this says I think I was wrong — which is the module's central error committed at the one moment the sentence has two reporters.

sentences.mnemonic: sē points at its own clause's subject.
